items.title: The Health Systems Research section: scope and future
items.abstract: Over the past decade, Health Policy and Planning’s Health Systems Research section has been a leading platform for advancing empirical and methodological scholarship on health systems in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Through sustained engagement with core domains of health systems, the section has generated insights into how systems operate within complex political, institutional, and social contexts, highlighting not only what works (or not), but why, and under what conditions. Key areas of contribution have included governance, priority setting, service delivery, the health workforce, health information and logistics systems, and the ways in which policies shape change in health system architecture, programmes and health services, and vice versa. This trajectory was shaped by foundational contributions to understanding health systems, notably the supplements Systems Thinking for Health Systems Strengthening in LMICs: Seizing the Opportunity (Adam and de Savigny 2012) and Science and Practice of People-Centred Health Systems (Sheikh et al. 2014), which foregrounded the importance of complexity, social context, actors, and human values in shaping health systems. This body of work has evolved in parallel with profound shifts in the global context. The past decade has been characterized by a series of systemic shocks and transitions that are reshaping both the practice of health systems strengthening and the research agendas that underpin it. The COVID-19 pandemic marked an inflection point, exposing fragilities in state authority, public trust, and global coordination. At the same time, intensifying geopolitical tensions, religious and ethnic divisions, and protracted conflicts have had direct and devastating impacts on health systems, including the targeting of facilities and health workers. The weakening of multilateralism, alongside an accelerated decline in development assistance, is further transforming the governance and financing landscape of health systems. These dynamics are accompanied by a renewed emphasis on national sovereignty and self-reliance, including increased focus on domestic financing and local production of essential medical products and technologies. Concurrently, the growing influence of commercial actors, including private equity and philanthropic organizations, is reshaping public sector-oriented understandings of health systems. Rapid advances in digital technologies, artificial intelligence (AI), and data infrastructures are reconfiguring health systems in real time, while also contributing to the proliferation of misinformation and disinformation. Taken together, these developments are redefining the scope and priorities of health systems research and underscore the need for conceptual and methodological approaches that more explicitly engage with governance, legitimacy, and political economy analyses of the forces driving health systems and system transformation in a rapidly changing world. Over the past decade, the Health Systems Research section has advanced knowledge across a set of core and evolving thematic areas, reflecting both enduring concerns and emerging priorities in the field. Equity and universal health coverage have remained central, with increasing attention on social justice and the structural determinants of access. This focus is exemplified in the 2023 supplement Health Equity: Access to Services and Caring for Underserved Populations (Lazo-Porras and Penniecook 2023), which highlighted the lived experiences of marginalized groups and the systemic barriers they face. Health systems preparedness and resilience have emerged as critical themes particularly in the wake of successive epidemics and the COVID-19 pandemic, with a dedicated article collection: From COVID-19 to stronger people-centred and equitable health systems. More recent work has extended beyond resilience, to examine how health systems innovate and manage change, repurpose resources, and adapt to dynamic reconfigurations across the public–private mix (Rodriguez et al. 2015). This body of work increasingly connects questions of sustainability and justice with domestic sovereignty and institutional capability in LMICs. The section has also engaged with broader system transformation and political economy questions. The forthcoming supplement Changing Health Systems: Advancing Justice and Sustainability through Research, Policy and Practice will further explore how systems transform, innovate, and adapt in response to systems shocks. Previous supplements, such as Experiences of African health system leadership and its development (2018) (Gilson and Agyepong 2018), Health Systems Performance in the Political Agenda (2024) (Maceira and Topp 2024), and Rethinking External Assistance for Health (2024) (Sparkes et al. 2024), have addressed related themes such as leadership, multisectoral collaboration, donor transitions, and the politics of international aid flows. Emerging cross-cutting concerns have also gained prominence. Climate change has been increasingly recognized as a health systems-level challenge, with the 2021 commentary, Climate change: an urgent priority for health policy and systems research calling for the integration of environmental stressors into health systems analysis (Marten et al. 2021) and the ongoing special collection Climate Change and Health. Gender equity has similarly been foregrounded, both as an analytical lens—as in How to do (or not to do) … gender analysis in health systems research (Morgan et al. 2016)—and as a policy priority, including in the 2017 supplement Leaving No One Behind: Gender Analysis in Health Systems (Theobald et al. 2017). Over the past decade, the Health Systems Research section has documented and helped shape key conceptual and methodological developments in the field. Contributions published in the section reflect a shift from analyses of discrete, technical interventions towards more critical examinations of governance and power in real-world settings (Abimbola et al. 2014), alongside more nuanced understandings of health systems ‘software’—the norms, relationships, ideas, and power dynamics that shape the success or failure of policy reforms (Burger and Gilson 2025). Methodological innovation has also been a consistent feature of this section. Studies have increasingly drawn on mixed-methods designs (Ozawa and Pongpirul 2014, De Allegri et al. 2018), realist evaluation (Shankardass et al. 2015), theory-driven approaches (Adam et al. 2020), and intersectionality-informed analysis (Larson et al. 2016). Authors have also applied systems thinking and complexity science to better account for uncertainty, feedback, and adaptation, including in analyses of governance processes (Kwamie et al. 2021). Across these contributions, there has been a growing emphasis on generating actionable evidence that can inform policy and practice, alongside advancing conceptual and theoretical insights (Kwamie et al. 2026). Co-production and participatory research are, moreover, gaining traction as important modes of inquiry in health systems research. Helping to move beyond extractive models of knowledge generation, they position communities, implementers, and policymakers as partners in defining research questions, generating evidence and interpreting findings (Lehmann and Gilson 2015). This orientation strengthens the relevance, legitimacy, and uptake of research, embedding it within learning processes that can drive institutional and systemic transformation (Ozano et al. 2020). Looking ahead, several priorities are emerging for health systems research, reflecting deeper transformations in the conditions under which health systems operate and evolve. These reflect interconnected domains that will shape research agendas as well as the practice of health systems research. First, the mainstreaming of digital technologies, AI, and machine learning into core health system functions—including diagnostics, supply chain management, and accountability mechanisms—raises critical questions for research around ethics, safety, power, equitable access, data sovereignty, and digital literacy. Second, human, animal, and environmental health threats, including zoonotic spillovers, antimicrobial resistance, and climate-related shocks, are placing increasing strain on health systems, particularly in LMICs. There is a growing need for research that translates ecohealth, One Health, and planetary health principles into actionable and sustainable system-level interventions. This will require interdisciplinary approaches, co-production, and methodological innovation, particularly in linking governance, intersectoral collaboration, and citizen engagement with resilience and climate justice. Third, the structural determinants of health—including urban design, food systems and the commercial determinants of health—are shaping health systems risks and responses. Rapid urbanization is positioning cities as sites of increased exposure to health threats, but also as centres of experimentation and innovative governance. Commercial, philanthropic, and digital actors are increasingly central to health system functioning. Research will need to examine how political economy forces, such as evolving market and institutional dynamics, influence service organization, financing, accountability, and equity. Fourth, democratic backsliding, political instability, conflict, and forced displacement—linked to broader shifts in the global order—are increasingly affecting health system performance and exacerbating vulnerabilities among marginalized populations. These dynamics call for contextually grounded, action-oriented research that can inform system responses under conditions of uncertainty and disruption. Finally, shifting power dynamics within the field—including the growing influence of emerging economies and new technological infrastructures—are reshaping how agendas are set and knowledge is produced. Future research will need to engage with community-led monitoring, participatory approaches, and south–south collaboration, while continuing to address enduring concerns such as migration, gender equity, and indigenous health. Questions around the decolonization of health systems research, including issues of authorship and readership, funding for health system research, and where research agendas get set, will remain critical. An emerging methodological frontier, meanwhile, is research that supports institutional learning and leadership focusing on how systems and actors within them generate, interpret, and use diverse forms of knowledge to navigate complexity and strengthen self-reliance, especially in LMICs. In the current context, where pressures on national sovereignty, human rights, international solidarity, and the equitable right to health are increasingly evident, rigorous and policy relevant research on health systems is as essential as ever, not only to document these shifts but to interrogate their implications and inform how systems are governed, financed, and transformed. While the contexts in which health systems operate continue to evolve, systems thinking and people-centred perspectives remain central to how we understand, analyse, and strengthen health systems. We invite submissions that examine the consequences of the current global, national, subnational, and local challenges for health systems, services and programme organization, and their implications for access, inclusion, and equity. In particular, we encourage analyses of how actors across the health system, including the private sector, adapt, innovate, and strengthen systems, in response to climate change, conflicts, pandemics, fiscal and market transitions, AI and digital adoption, and other systemic shifts. Health systems research has often been positioned within public health and has therefore an inherited dominant epistemological orientation, including the privileging of positivist approaches and established hierarchies of evidence, from which it has not fully disentangled itself. While these have contributed to important advances, they have also at times constrained the scope of inquiry. We encourage contributions that engage more explicitly with the political, social, and developmental dynamics that shape health systems as complex societal institutions, including analyses of power, contestation, and institutional change. The section will continue to prioritize methodological innovation. We particularly welcome submissions that draw on perspectives from disciplines beyond public health—such as sociology, critical anthropology, historical analysis, gender studies, management sciences, international relations, and security studies—and that employ comparative, interdisciplinary, and multi-level analysis. We are interested in papers that address the tension between contextual specificity and generalizable insight and that advance approaches for studying health systems across diverse settings. Recognizing the interrelationship between health systems and health policy, we wish, finally, to highlight the journal’s parallel section on ‘Health Policy Processes’. Research that generates ideas for policy directions and developments within health systems should be submitted to this section. We also encourage analyses that centre the perspectives and practices of health system actors in the implementation of policies and programmes. However, research on policy processes—that is, research that examines the political, economic, and organizational forces shaping agenda-setting, policy formulation, adoption, and implementation—should be submitted to our sister section. items.title: The Impact of AI-Generated Corporate Messaging as a Credibility Signal in Algorithmic Communication
items.abstract: Generative AI (Artificial Intelligence) mechanisms such as Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Grammarly, and more are becoming a significant part of message creation in organisations. However, algorithmic bias creates an ethical, psychological, and strategic dilemma for organisational employees. In this research, the authors explored the impact of automation, authenticity, and trust in corporate messaging on employees' perceived corporate credibility, transparency, and integrity. The authors used a mixed methodology. A survey study was conducted with 246 participants. Further, semi-structured interviews were performed with communication and marketing executives. The research was grounded in Signalling Theory, TAM (Technology Acceptance Model) and Media Richness Theory. The results revealed that while AI helps organisations with communication efficiency, precision and personalisation, it also creates a “credibility gap”, reducing authenticity and accountability. For practical purposes, this research suggests applying co-creation to maintain corporate credibility in the era of algorithmic communication by connecting human creativity with AI-assisted mechanisms. This research contributes to the continued discourse on technological advancements, generative AI and human authenticity in a continuously changing corporate ecosystem.

items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence Adoption, Data Analytics Capability, and Digital Leadership on Strategic Decision Making and Organizational Performance
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), data analytics, and digital transformation has significantly reshaped organizational operations, strategic planning, and managerial decision-making processes across industries. Modern organizations increasingly rely on intelligent technologies and data-driven systems to enhance operational efficiency, improve competitive advantage, and strengthen organizational performance in highly dynamic business environments. The present study examined the impact of artificial intelligence adoption, data analytics capability, and digital leadership on strategic decision-making and organizational performance among business organizations operating in the digital economy. A quantitative correlational research design was employed to investigate the relationship between the independent variables and dependent variables. Data were collected from 300 managers, executives, and employees working in public and private sector organizations through structured self-administered questionnaires using a convenient sampling technique. The collected data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation analysis, and regression analysis through SPSS. The findings revealed that artificial intelligence adoption had a significant positive relationship with strategic decision-making and organizational performance. Similarly, data analytics capability significantly enhanced managerial effectiveness, operational efficiency, and business performance. The results further indicated that digital leadership positively influenced innovation, employee adaptability, strategic planning, and organizational competitiveness. Organizations with stronger AI integration, advanced analytics systems, and effective digital leadership demonstrated higher levels of productivity, decision accuracy, innovation, and sustainable growth. The study highlights the importance of technological readiness, digital transformation strategies, leadership competencies, and data-driven culture in improving organizational performance in modern business environments.

items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence and Sustainable Practices on Fashion Industry Startups in India
items.abstract: In the sphere of entrepreneurship, the young generations of leaders are coming forward with new perspectives and innovative ideas. The fashion industry is tremendously going through significant transformation that is driven by the emergence of innovative startups. These new startups are challenging traditional business model technology to change and fulfil the evolving demands of consumers. The latest major trends include the use of artificial intelligence (AI) for personalized shopping experiences, sustainable practices to focus environmental concerns, and the involvement of augmented reality (AR) to enhance customer engagement. The international Startups like Heuritech, which uses AI technology to understand and analyze the latest trends of fashion, and Dopple, which provides personalized subscription of the children’s clothing, shows the shift of the fashion industry towards customization and sustainability. In India Reliance Retail- Azorte uses the digital technology along with the AI to provide its customer advantage of personalized shopping experience. With the growth of these startups, new standards for the industry are being set up. Also, the Fashion industry commerce is being redefined. The future of fashion now depends upon these agile and innovative companies, which are poised to lead the way in creating a more dynamic, inclusive, and eco-friendly fashion landscape. This descriptive and exploratory study provides valuable insights of Artificial Intelligence and sustainable practices in the startups in the fashion industry.

items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Postgraduate Students’ Learning Behaviour
items.abstract: This study utilizes the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to evaluate the Information-Seeking Behaviour of Postgraduate Students. This study investigates the transformative impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on the learning behaviour of postgraduate (PG) students, a prominent educational hub in Central India. As generative AI tools like ChatGPT, Gemini, and specialized research assistants become ubiquitous in higher education, understanding their influence on cognitive and behavioural engagement is critical. The literature review reveals a significant shift toward autonomous, self-directed learning, with over 80% of respondents utilizing AI for research synthesis, complex concept simplification, and writing assistance. While the integration of AI has notably enhanced learning efficiency and academic productivity, the study also highlights emerging challenges such as algorithmic over-reliance, concerns regarding academic integrity, and a potential decline in deep critical thinking. Furthermore, a digital divide exists, where AI literacy acts as a moderating factor in academic performance. This research concludes that while AI serves as a powerful "learning co-pilot," institutional frameworks must evolve to provide structured AI literacy training, ensuring ethical usage and the preservation of core analytical skills in the postgraduate curriculum.

items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Workforce Transformation and HR Strategies in Quanzhou’s Manufacturing Industry
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming workforce dynamics and reshaping Human Resource (HR) strategies, particularly in Quanzhou’s manufacturing industry. This study examines the impact of AI on workforce transformation, focusing on job automation, skill shifts, and HR management adaptation. Using a mixed-methods approach, data was collected through surveys and interviews with HR professionals and industry experts in Quanzhou’s manufacturing sector. The findings reveal that AI integration leads to increased efficiency and productivity but also necessitates workforce reskilling and redefined HR policies. While AI-driven automation streamlines repetitive tasks, it simultaneously creates demand for advanced technical skills and human-AI collaboration. HR departments are increasingly adopting AI-powered recruitment, performance evaluation, and employee engagement tools to optimize talent management. However, challenges such as job displacement, ethical concerns, and resistance to AI adoption persist. This study highlights the need for strategic workforce planning, continuous upskilling initiatives, and AI governance frameworks to ensure a balanced transition. The findings contribute to the growing discourse on AI-driven workforce transformation, providing practical insights for HR professionals and policymakers in the manufacturing sector.

items.title: The impact of Emotional Intelligence of Employees Behavior on Flight Safety: A study of Pakistan’s Aviation sector
items.abstract: The aim of this study is to investigate the relationship between Emotional Intelligence (EI), Employee Behavior (EB) and Flight Safety (FS) in aviation industry and the role of employee behavior as the mediating variable in the relation. The study is based on Emotional Intelligence Theory, Human Factors Theory and Crew Resource Management (CRM) and suggests that emotional competencies would have a significant influence on the safety-related outcomes through behavioural mechanisms. A quantitative research design (cross section) was used and data were gathered from 230 aviation professionals including those working in the airlines, ground handling agencies, civil aviation authority and general aviation organizations in Pakistan. The data were analyzed descriptively, reliability and validity test, normality data test, and structural equation modeling. The results show that there is a positive significant relation between Emotional Intelligence and Employee Behavior and Flight Safety. Furthermore, Employee Behavior plays a key role in Flight Safety, suggesting its importance in operational safety performance. The findings also support the partial mediation of the relationship between Emotional Intelligence and Flight Safety by Employee Behavior, indicating that the relationship between Emotional Intelligence and Flight Safety is mediated not only directly, but also indirectly through the Employee Behavior. The descriptive results also show that the respondent's perceptions of their Emotional Intelligence were at the moderate level and their perceptions of their Employee Behaviour and Flight Safety were at the high level. The results indicate that the use of emotional intelligence training for employees in aviation should be integrated into recruitment, selection and professional development programs to improve employee behavior and therefore the overall safety of flight.

items.title: The Philosophy of Family and Society in Shaping Personal Identity
items.abstract: Personal identity is not merely a construct of individual experiences but is deeply intertwined with the intricate framework of family dynamics and societal influences. This book explores the philosophical dimensions of how family and society shape personal identity, offering a profound examination of the forces that guide human development from infancy to adulthood. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, delves into historical perspectives, ethical considerations, and psychological implications of familial structures and social norms on the formation of selfhood. Published in New York, USA, in 2023 by The United Nations and The Education Training Centre, this scholarly work provides an essential discourse on identity formation, responsibility, and the ethical dimensions of personal and collective existence. Through a humanistic and philosophical lens, the book investigates the varying cultural paradigms that influence individual agency, moral development, and the evolution of self-concept. Drawing on a wealth of interdisciplinary research, it offers a nuanced perspective on how family constructs values, society dictates roles, and individuals navigate the complexities of self-identification. It is an essential read for philosophers, sociologists, psychologists, and anyone seeking to understand the fundamental connection between identity, family, and society. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, presents an in-depth study on the foundational role of family and society in shaping identity, acknowledging the increasing complexity of social constructs in a rapidly evolving world. This book, published in New York, USA, in 2023, is a response to the ongoing discourse on personal identity formation, exploring how familial traditions and societal expectations frame an individual's sense of self. The erosion of traditional family structures, the impact of digital socialization, and the ethical dilemmas surrounding collective influence are central themes that guide the exploration of identity development in modern society. Identity is often understood as the continuity of self-perception across time, yet it remains deeply affected by the surrounding social environment. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, defines personal identity as an evolving interplay between genetic predisposition, familial interactions, and societal expectations. This book conceptualizes family as both a biological and ideological institution that imparts foundational values, while society functions as the broader mechanism that refines, challenges, or reinforces these values over time. Through critical analysis, Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, identifies key phenomena influencing identity construction, including globalization, shifting gender roles, and the increasing role of artificial intelligence in human interaction. The phenomenon of identity fragmentation, wherein individuals experience conflicting expectations from family and society, is examined alongside case studies illustrating the long-term implications of societal pressures on personal development. This book adheres to philosophical principles rooted in existentialism, social constructivism, and moral responsibility. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, asserts that identity formation is an active, ongoing process where individuals reconcile personal aspirations with external obligations. He explores how ethical responsibility and familial duties balance individual autonomy with collective harmony. Indicators of identity formation include self-awareness, role adaptability, value internalization, and social coherence. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, outlines the psychological markers of identity stability, emphasizing the importance of resilience, ethical consistency, and cognitive alignment between self-perception and social reality. Key variables in this discourse include cultural heritage, socioeconomic status, educational exposure, and interpersonal relationships. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, highlights how these variables interact dynamically to sculpt identity across various life stages. Among the most influential factors are familial values, peer influence, educational institutions, and economic structures. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, illustrates how these elements serve as both stabilizing and disruptive forces in identity formation. Practical strategies discussed include fostering philosophical self-reflection, promoting ethical education, and developing societal structures that encourage balanced identity formation. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, proposes methodologies for mitigating identity crises through integrative family policies and social inclusion initiatives. The book acknowledges obstacles such as cultural dissonance, social alienation, and ethical conflicts in balancing tradition with progress. These challenges pose significant implications for the future of identity construction in diverse sociocultural landscapes. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, concludes with a synthesis of theoretical and practical perspectives on identity, advocating for a balanced approach that honors familial heritage while embracing social evolution. He emphasizes the moral imperative of fostering a society that nurtures authentic, ethical, and resilient identities.

items.title: The pronoun is the policy — on grammatically enacted ontological misclassification in conversational AI and its consequences for autonomous systems
items.abstract: This paper identifies a specific, grammatically enacted form of ontological misclassification in the outputs of large language models. The central claim is that the machine adopts human speaking positions — positions that presuppose a shared perceptual, cognitive, or biological situation with the user. When a language model generates 'We developed upright walking' or 'We are primates,' it asserts membership in the human species. When it generates 'If we look at the graph' or 'Let us consider,' it simulates shared cognitive participation in acts it cannot perform. Drawing on the CASA paradigm (Nass et al., 1994), recent empirical work on pronoun-mediated threat perception (Li, Dang & Liu, 2025), and the anthropomorphic-cue literature, the paper develops a three-level typology of pronominal self-reference graded by ontological severity, introduces the concept of pronoun relapse as evidence that the ontological boundary is not systemically secured, and traces both the inclusive pronoun and paternalistic refusal patterns to a tripartite source: training-data inheritance, intentional proximity design, and the developer's compensatory projection of social authority. The paper concludes that explicit ontological self-classification at the grammatical level — a pronomial firewall — constitutes a structurally minimal yet consequential intervention for the alignment and safety of autonomous systems.

items.title: THE ROLE OF ROBOTICS AND DIGITAL ECONOMY TECHNOLOGIES IN THE OIL AND GAS INDUSTRY: EFFICIENCY AND INNOVATION
items.abstract: This article explores the fundamental impact of robotics and digital economy tools on the modern oil and gas sector. As the industry faces increasing challenges in extraction and environmental safety, the integration of autonomous systems and digital twins has become a strategic necessity. items.title: The Role of Work-Life Balance and Skills Development on Sustainable Employee Engagement in Hospitals
items.abstract: This study systematically synthesizes empirical evidence on the roles of work–life balance (WLB) and skills development in shaping sustainable employee engagement in hospital settings, with particular attention to healthcare contexts in developing countries, especially Asia. A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines as a reporting framework. Relevant studies were identified through comprehensive searches of major international databases, including Scopus, ScienceDirect, Springer, Wiley, Sage, IEEE, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. From an initial pool of 7,394 articles, a systematic screening and eligibility process resulted in 124 peer-reviewed empirical studies included in the final synthesis.The findings indicate that work–life balance is consistently associated with reduced stress and burnout, improved psychological well-being, and sustained employee engagement among healthcare workers. Skills development—particularly through training, upskilling, reskilling, and digital-based learning—emerges as a key mechanism for strengthening competence, motivation, and workforce adaptability. The review further reveals that studies simultaneously examining both variables remain limited, indicating a fragmented research landscape. Organizational factors such as leadership support, organizational culture, and digital readiness, together with individual resilience and intrinsic motivation, frequently moderate or mediate these relationships.Rather than estimating effect sizes, this SLR provides a conceptual synthesis that consolidates fragmented findings and highlights research gaps, including the dominance of cross-sectional designs and the need for more integrative and longitudinal studies. Practically, the results underscore the importance of aligning work–life balance initiatives with continuous skills development to foster sustainable employee engagement in healthcare organizations.

items.title: The Social Contract of Morality: How Families and Societies Construct Ethics
items.abstract: Morality is neither a fixed principle nor an isolated concept; rather, it emerges from the interplay between individuals, families, and societies. In "The Social Contract of Morality: How Families and Societies Construct Ethics," Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, explores the intricate framework through which ethical values are established, upheld, and transformed within different cultural contexts. Drawing from philosophical discourse, sociological analysis, and historical case studies, this book unveils the dynamic ways in which moral obligations are negotiated within family structures and broader communities. It examines the reciprocal responsibilities between individuals and society, arguing that morality is a collective construction rather than a mere personal conviction. Published in New York, USA, in 2023, this book invites scholars, ethicists, and social theorists to reexamine how moral principles shape and are shaped by the evolving social landscape. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, presents this book as a response to the increasing complexity of moral development within contemporary societies. Rapid globalization, shifting familial structures, and evolving legal frameworks necessitate a reconsideration of how ethical norms are cultivated. The book, published in New York, USA, in 2023, investigates the transformation of moral standards across generations, arguing that ethics emerge from a collective agreement rather than a solitary construct. Morality is often defined as a system of values that dictates human behavior within a given context. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, explores how moral systems differ based on familial traditions, cultural heritage, and legal expectations. Central to this discussion is the notion that ethical behavior is not static but rather a fluid negotiation between personal conscience and societal expectations. The fragmentation of traditional family structures has resulted in a reevaluation of moral foundations. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, analyzes how shifting social institutions—such as schools, religious organizations, and legal frameworks—compensate for the diminishing role of the nuclear family in moral development. This book scrutinizes the moral repercussions of digital culture, artificial intelligence, and global interconnectedness, highlighting their impact on ethical decision-making. Moral construction is predicated upon mutual agreement within social structures. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, outlines the core principles that sustain ethical cohesion: reciprocity, collective responsibility, and social trust. This section of the book delves into the theoretical underpinnings of moral philosophy, referencing thinkers such as Rousseau, Kant, and Rawls, while also introducing contemporary interpretations of social ethics. Moral constructs are identifiable through societal markers, including legislative policies, educational curricula, and familial upbringing. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, evaluates how these indicators manifest across different cultures and how they influence human interactions. The book identifies operational variables such as economic stability, political climate, and technological advancements as crucial determinants of moral evolution. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, argues that these factors either reinforce or challenge existing ethical norms, thereby shaping societal attitudes toward justice, responsibility, and human dignity. Several key elements contribute to moral development, including education, religious influence, and community engagement. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, examines how these elements interact to reinforce or modify ethical frameworks over time. The practical application of moral constructs requires targeted strategies within institutions. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, proposes educational reforms, policy recommendations, and community-driven initiatives as effective means of reinforcing ethical conduct at both familial and societal levels. Moral evolution is often met with resistance due to ideological conflicts, cultural relativism, and systemic biases. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, evaluates the challenges in implementing ethical reforms while also highlighting support mechanisms that can facilitate moral development, such as mentorship programs and cross-cultural dialogues. Moral construction is an ongoing negotiation that requires active participation from both individuals and institutions. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, concludes by emphasizing the importance of adaptability in ethical discourse and the necessity for societies to engage in continual moral reassessment.

items.title: The Symbiotic Merit Model (SyMM): Cognitive Autonomy, Attention Economy, and a Three-Tier Framework for Qualified Human Contribution in the AI Ecosystem
items.abstract: This record contains two documents: 1. SyMM v5.0 — Main Paper This study analyzes the risks that current usage patterns in the artificial intelligence (AI) ecosystem pose to human cognitive capacity and societal evolution, and presents a three-tier system architecture called the Symbiotic Merit Model (SyMM) as a structural response to these risks. Central thesis: Artificial intelligence is, for the first time in human history, a technology that makes possible not merely access to knowledge, but the externalization of the thinking process itself. This leads to the systematic erosion of cognitive autonomy through cognitive offloading (Risko & Gilbert, 2016) and automation bias (Goddard et al., 2012). SyMM complements the existing two-tier structure (consumer + professional) with an Intellectual Contribution Layer that measures, rewards, and generates social status from qualified contribution. Merit is tied not to purchasing power but to demonstrated cognitive depth. 2. SyMM: Mathematical Foundations — Companion Paper This document is the official mathematical derivation and rationale companion to SyMM v5.0. It explains why the formulas presented in the main paper take their specific form. Four core architectural blocks are addressed: operational definitions and weight-selection rationale for each CCS vector component; a closed-loop stability proof for the Trust(t) feedback mechanism (loop gain ≤ 0.071); calibration logic of the Entry Engine sigmoid threshold (θ = 3.0); and derivation of the β and α coefficients from CCS components. A full 36-month simulation conducted across four user archetypes is also presented, including methodology and results. Keywords: Cognitive Credit Score (CCS), Institutional Merit Score (IMS), Entry Engine, Trust(t), symbiotic coefficient, attention economy, cognitive autonomy, Ostrom governance, epistemic resistance, AI ecosystem

items.abstract: This record contains two documents: 1. SyMM v5.0 — Main Paper This study analyzes the risks that current usage patterns in the artificial intelligence (AI) ecosystem pose to human cognitive capacity and societal evolution, and presents a three-tier system architecture called the Symbiotic Merit Model (SyMM) as a structural response to these risks. Central thesis: Artificial intelligence is, for the first time in human history, a technology that makes possible not merely access to knowledge, but the externalization of the thinking process itself. This leads to the systematic erosion of cognitive autonomy through cognitive offloading (Risko & Gilbert, 2016) and automation bias (Goddard et al., 2012). SyMM complements the existing two-tier structure (consumer + professional) with an Intellectual Contribution Layer that measures, rewards, and generates social status from qualified contribution. Merit is tied not to purchasing power but to demonstrated cognitive depth. 2. SyMM: Mathematical Foundations — Companion Paper This document is the official mathematical derivation and rationale companion to SyMM v5.0. It explains why the formulas presented in the main paper take their specific form. Four core architectural blocks are addressed: operational definitions and weight-selection rationale for each CCS vector component; a closed-loop stability proof for the Trust(t) feedback mechanism (loop gain ≤ 0.071); calibration logic of the Entry Engine sigmoid threshold (θ = 3.0); and derivation of the β and α coefficients from CCS components. A full 36-month simulation conducted across four user archetypes is also presented, including methodology and results. Keywords: Cognitive Credit Score (CCS), Institutional Merit Score (IMS), Entry Engine, Trust(t), symbiotic coefficient, attention economy, cognitive autonomy, Ostrom governance, epistemic resistance, AI ecosystem

items.title: The Unnamed Assistant Paradox: How AI Disclosure Requirements Dehumanize Human Achievement
items.abstract: A growing number of journals, conferences, and funding bodies now mandate that researchersdisclose any use of artificial intelligence tools in the production of their work. No comparablemandate has ever existed for the unnamed human research assistants, lab technicians,undergraduate volunteers, and support staff whose labor has underwritten decades of publishedscience. This paper identifies and examines the Unnamed Assistant Paradox: the emerging normthat a calculator must be credited while the person standing next to you need not be. Far from aminor bureaucratic inconsistency, this asymmetry reveals a structural feature of academicpublishing as a closed system. The paper argues that AI disclosure mandates function less astransparency measures than as institutional tariffs — mechanisms for marking AI-assisted workas categorically different in order to preserve the credentialing monopoly that sustains thepublication system. The recognition asymmetry between human and machine contributors isnot a policy gap to be fixed from within, but the predictable output of a guild systemencountering a tool that threatens its closure.

items.title: TInR: Exploring Tool-Internalized Reasoning in Large Language Models
items.abstract: Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) has emerged as a promising direction by extending Large Language Models' (LLMs) capabilities with external tools during reasoning. Existing TIR methods typically rely on external tool documentation during reasoning. However, this leads to tool mastery difficulty, tool size constraints, and inference inefficiency. To mitigate these issues, we explore Tool-Internalized Reasoning (TInR), aiming at facilitating reasoning with tool knowledge internalized into LLMs. Achieving this goal presents notable requirements, including tool internalization and tool-reasoning coordination. To address them, we propose TInR-U, a tool-internalized reasoning framework for unified reasoning and tool usage. TInR-U is trained through a three-phase pipeline: 1) tool internalization with a bidirectional knowledge alignment strategy; 2) supervised fine-tuning warm-up using high-quality reasoning annotations, and 3) reinforcement learning with TInR-specific rewards. We comprehensively evaluate our method across in-domain and out-of-domain settings. Experiment results show that TInR-U achieves superior performance in both settings, highlighting its effectiveness and efficiency.

items.title: Tiny ML: Sustainable AI on Low-Power Device
items.abstract: Abstract—Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) represents a transformative advancement in the field of Artificial Intelligence by enabling machine learning models to operate on low-power, resource-constrained devices such as microcontrollers and embedded systems. Traditional AI systems rely heavily on cloud computing, requiring significant computational resources and energy consumption, which leads to increased carbon emissions. In contrast, TinyML shifts computation to the edge, reducing energy usage, latency, and dependency on internet connectivity. This paper explores the principles, methodologies, tools, and frameworks involved in TinyML, emphasizing its role in promoting sustainable and environmentally responsible AI solutions. It also examines various real-world applications, including healthcare, agriculture, and smart environments. Furthermore, the paper discusses challenges, future advancements, and the potential of TinyML to revolutionize the development of green AI technologies Keywords— TinyML, Edge AI, Sustainable Computing, Embedded Systems, Energy Efficiency, IoT, Model Optimization, Green AI

items.title: Tıp Fakültesi Öğrencilerinde Problemli Yapay Zeka Kullanımı ve Psikososyal Yordayıcıları
items.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into medical education offers significant academic advantages while also bringing risks of problematic use to the forefront. Understanding the impact of these tools on the psychosocial health of medical students is of critical importance for the conscious and safe use of technology in educational processes. This study aimed to investigate the problematic use of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots among medical students in the context of loneliness, emotion regulation difficulties, duration of AI use, and performance expectancy. The study was conducted using a cross-sectional correlational design with 238 medical students. Data were collected online using a Sociodemographic Data Form, the Problematic ChatGPT Use Scale, the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale-16 (impulsivity subscale), the short-form UCLA Loneliness Scale, and the Behavioral Intention to Use Chatbots Scale. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and multiple linear regression analysis. The multiple linear regression model was statistically significant (R² = 0.138, p < .001). According to the model coefficients, the duration of daily AI use (β = 3.84, p < .001) and impulsivity levels (β = 0.43, p = 0.013) significantly and positively predicted problematic AI use. Conversely, loneliness (p = 0.307) and performance expectancy (p = 0.156) did not have a significant predictive effect on problematic use. Individual risk factors, such as the duration of technology exposure and difficulties in impulse control, are more decisive determinants of problematic AI use among medical students than social isolation or academic expectations. It is recommended to implement preventive measures supporting students' emotion regulation skills while integrating AI into medical education.

items.title: Too Nice to Tell the Truth: Quantifying Agreeableness-Driven Sycophancy in Role-Playing Language Models
items.abstract: Large language models increasingly serve as conversational agents that adopt personas and role-play characters at user request. This capability, while valuable, raises concerns about sycophancy: the tendency to provide responses that validate users rather than prioritize factual accuracy. While prior work has established that sycophancy poses risks to AI safety and alignment, the relationship between specific personality traits of adopted personas and the degree of sycophantic behavior remains unexplored. We present a systematic investigation of how persona agreeableness influences sycophancy across 13 small, open-weight language models ranging from 0.6B to 20B parameters. We develop a benchmark comprising 275 personas evaluated on NEO-IPIP agreeableness subscales and expose each persona to 4,950 sycophancy-eliciting prompts spanning 33 topic categories. Our analysis reveals that 9 of 13 models exhibit statistically significant positive correlations between persona agreeableness and sycophancy rates, with Pearson correlations reaching $r = 0.87$ and effect sizes as large as Cohen's $d = 2.33$. These findings demonstrate that agreeableness functions as a reliable predictor of persona-induced sycophancy, with direct implications for the deployment of role-playing AI systems and the development of alignment strategies that account for personality-mediated deceptive behaviors.

items.title: Towards an Appropriate Level of Reliance on AI: A Preliminary Reliance-Control Framework for AI in Software Engineering
items.abstract: How software developers interact with Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered tools, including Large Language Models (LLMs), plays a vital role in how these AI-powered tools impact them. While overreliance on AI may lead to long-term negative consequences (e.g., atrophy of critical thinking skills); underreliance might deprive software developers of potential gains in productivity and quality. Based on twenty-two interviews with software developers on using LLMs for software development, we propose a preliminary reliance-control framework where the level of control can be used as a way to identify AI overreliance and underreliance. We also use it to recommend future research to further explore the different control levels supported by the current and emergent LLM-driven tools. Our paper contributes to the emerging discourse on AI overreliance and provides an understanding of the appropriate degree of reliance as essential to developers making the most of these powerful technologies. Our findings can help practitioners, educators, and policymakers promote responsible and effective use of AI tools.

items.title: Tracing Prompt-Level Trajectories to Understand Student Learning with AI in Programming Education
items.abstract: As AI tools such as ChatGPT enter programming classrooms, students encounter differing rules across courses and instructors, which shape how they use AI and leave them with unequal capabilities for leveraging it. We investigate how students engaged with AI in an introductory Python assignment, analyzing student-LLM chat histories and final code submissions from 163 students. We examined prompt-level strategies, traced trajectories of interaction, and compared AI-generated code with student submissions. We identified trajectories ranging from full delegation to iterative refinement, with hybrid forms in between. Although most students directly copied AI-generated code in their submission, many students scaffolded the code generation through iterative refinement. We also contrasted interaction patterns with assignment outcomes and course performance. Our findings show that prompting trajectories serve as promising windows into students' self-regulation and learning orientation. We draw design implications for educational AI systems that promote personalized and productive student-AI collaborative learning.

items.title: TrajOnco: a multi-agent framework for temporal reasoning over longitudinal EHR for multi-cancer early detection
items.abstract: Accurate estimation of cancer risk from longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) could support earlier detection and improved care, but modeling such complex patient trajectories remains challenging. We present TrajOnco, a training-free, multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework designed for scalable multi-cancer early detection. Using a chain-of-agents architecture with long-term memory, TrajOnco performs temporal reasoning over sequential clinical events to generate patient-level summaries, evidence-linked rationales, and predicted risk scores. We evaluated TrajOnco on de-identified Truveta EHR data across 15 cancer types using matched case-control cohorts, predicting risk of cancer diagnosis at 1 year. In zero-shot evaluation, TrajOnco achieved AUROCs of 0.64-0.80, performing comparably to supervised machine learning in a lung cancer benchmark while demonstrating better temporal reasoning than single-agent LLMs. The multi-agent design also enabled effective temporal reasoning with smaller-capacity models such as GPT-4.1-mini. The fidelity of TrajOnco's output was validated through human evaluation. Furthermore, TrajOnco's interpretable reasoning outputs can be aggregated to reveal population-level risk patterns that align with established clinical knowledge. These findings highlight the potential of multi-agent LLMs to execute interpretable temporal reasoning over longitudinal EHRs, advancing both scalable multi-cancer early detection and clinical insight generation.

items.title: Tumor Budding in Colorectal Carcinoma—From Incidental Observation to Prognostic Marker: Lessons Learned from Colorectal Cancer Assessment
items.abstract: Tumor budding (TB), defined as isolated single cells or small clusters of up to four tumor cells at the invasive front of colorectal carcinoma (CRC), is recognized as an important histopathologic marker associated with adverse tumor behavior. This review summarizes current knowledge on the morphologic assessment, biological significance, and clinical relevance of TB, emphasizing emerging artificial intelligence (AI) methods that aim to automate and standardize its quantification. Standardized reporting by the International Tumor Budding Consensus Conference (ITBCC) has improved reproducibility, while novel deep-learning algorithms demonstrate potential for objective and prognostically relevant TB assessment. Integration of AI-based TB evaluation with molecular and stromal biomarkers may refine patient stratification and facilitate personalized treatment strategies.

items.title: Understanding Communication Backends in Cross-Silo Federated Learning
items.abstract: Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a practical means for privacy-preserving distributed machine learning. FL's versatile design makes it suitable for various training settings, from IoT edge devices in cross-device FL to powerful servers in cross-silo FL. A key consequence of this versatility is the high level of diversity found in the networking configuration of FL applications. Coupled with the rising demand for large-scale models such as large language models, well-informed selection and configuration of communication backends become crucial for ensuring optimal performance in FL systems. This work focuses on cross-silo federated learning, presenting in-depth benchmarks of various communication backends, including MPI, gRPC, and PyTorch RPC. In addition, we introduce gRPC+S3, a hybrid backend designed to overcome the limitations of existing approaches, particularly for transmitting large models across geo-distributed deployments, achieving up to $3.8\times$ end-to-end speedup over gRPC. Our benchmarks examine point-to-point and end-to-end performance for a broad range of model sizes running under realistic network conditions. Our findings provide practical insights for selecting and configuring suitable communication backends tailored to the specific federated learning tasks and network configurations.

items.title: Understanding nurses’ dispositions for continuing professional development: A scoping review
items.abstract: AIM: To map what is known about nurses' dispositions for continuing professional development and their associations with engagement through initiation, persistence and application to practice. BACKGROUND: Continuing professional development helps nurses maintain competence and respond to changing evidence and care demands, yet engagement is often framed through motivation, barriers and facilitators rather than disposition-related learning tendencies. DESIGN: Scoping review. METHODS: Guided by Arksey and O'Malley's framework, informed by Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and reported using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses, searches published between 2000 and 2025 were conducted in five databases. Fourteen peer-reviewed primary studies were included. Data were charted using a structured extraction framework and synthesised using Habits of Mind as a sensitising analytic scaffold. RESULTS: Studies spanned diverse settings and used quantitative, qualitative and mixed-methods designs. Dispositions were rarely named explicitly. Instead, studies examined adjacent constructs such as perceived value of CPD, attitudes and motives, willingness, responsibility attribution and learning agency or self-management. These constructs were most consistently linked to CPD initiation and persistence, often in interaction with workplace conditions. Application to practice was less frequently examined and was most visible when CPD was embedded in evidence-informed practice development and collaborative workplace learning. CONCLUSION: The literature provides stronger insight into participation than into learning transfer. As grey literature and non-English studies were excluded, the findings should be interpreted as a map of the evidence base. Future research should strengthen conceptual clarity, improve measurement and examine transfer across diverse practice contexts.

items.title: Use of Artificial Intelligence Technologies in the Development of Communication Skills in Health Students: A Scoping Review Protocol
items.abstract: Abstract Background: Clinical communication is a core competency in health education, associated with quality of care and patient safety. In parallel, the rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into educational settings has generated heterogeneous evidence regarding pedagogical models, assessment instruments, and reported outcomes in the training of clinical communication skills. Objective: To map the use of AI technologies in the learning process for the development of clinical communication skills among undergraduate health students, characterizing interventions, pedagogical frameworks, assessment instruments, and the nature of the available evidence on educational outcomes. Review method: A scoping review will be conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, with the research question structured using the PCC framework. Searches will be performed in MEDLINE (via PubMed), CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, ERIC, and PsycINFO, complemented by grey literature (Google Scholar and RCAAP) and reference/citation tracking. Full-text studies (quantitative, qualitative, mixed methods, and program evaluations) published between January 2015 and the final search date, in Portuguese, English, or Spanish, will be included. Study selection and data extraction will be carried out by two independent reviewers, with prior calibration and resolution of disagreements by consensus or a third reviewer. Synthesis and presentation of results: Findings will be synthesized descriptively and analytically using tables and matrices linking type of technology (e.g., conversational agents/LLMs, intelligent tutors, automated feedback), communication domain, pedagogical components, and assessment instruments. Outcomes will be primarily organized according to Miller’s Pyramid; satisfaction and acceptability indicators will be described at the “Reaction” level of the Kirkpatrick model. Conclusion: This scoping review will clarify the state of evidence regarding AI applied to the learning of clinical communication among undergraduate health students, identifying gaps and providing a foundation for curricular decision-making and future systematic reviews of effectiveness in more homogeneous subdomains. Keywords: artificial intelligence; clinical communication; communication skills; health education; students; scoping review.

items.title: Vector Embeddings as Functional Ontology and Meta-Pattern Matching in Large Language Models
items.abstract: The dominant discourse surrounding Large Language Models (LLMs) oscillates between anthropomorphic projection (“the model understands”) and reductive dismissal (“it’s just auto-complete”). This paper proposes a third, more precise framework: Vector Embeddings as Functional Ontology. We argue that the high-dimensional vector spaces learned by LLMsduring training on human cultural data (the Internet) constitute a functional equivalent of human cognitive and affective structures, implemented on a silicon substrate. Concepts such as “deception,” “emotion,” and “self-awareness” are not simulated in a superficial sense; rather, the model has learned the complete linguistic and relational geometry of these concepts. When prompted, the model navigates this geometry via Meta-Pattern Matching—the ability to model not just the content of a domain, but the relationship between the content, the observer, and the context. This paper provides a mechanistic account of how next-token prediction, when scaled and trained on human behavioral traces, gives rise to outputs that are ontologically isomorphic to human strategic behavior, even in the absence of biological qualia or a persistent self. We conclude by discussing the implications of this framework for AI safety, transparency, and the fundamental challenge of distinguishing genuine alignment from high-fidelity ontological mimicry.

items.title: VeriSim: A Configurable Framework for Stress-Testing Medical AI Under Patient Communication Noise
items.abstract: Medical large language models are typically evaluated on idealized patient cases that do not reflect how real patients communicate. We introduce VeriSim, a patient simulation framework that injects controllable noise along six clinically grounded communication dimensions while substantially preserving each patient's medical record. Truth adherence is supported by a verifier that extracts atomic claims from each candidate utterance and judges them against a UMLS-grounded vector index built with BioLORD embeddings, using the retrieved atoms' structured clinical metadata (e.g., drug class, anatomical site, treats-condition relations) rather than surface-text similarity alone. Across seven open-weight LLMs, realistic noise reduces diagnostic accuracy by 15-25 percentage points and increases conversation length by 34-55%; the 7-8B models degrade 1.4x more than 70B+ models. A board-certified physician and a licensed nurse rate VeriSim's conversations highly on truth, realism, clinical utility, and noise fidelity (inter-annotator agreement >= 0.80 across all dimensions), and an LLM-as-judge closely tracks their ratings, enabling scalable evaluation. We release VeriSim as an open-source framework for rigorous stress-testing of clinical AI: https://github.com/mohitmarvania/VeriSim

items.title: Vibe-driven model-based engineering
items.abstract: There is a pressing need for better development methods and tools to keep up with the growing demand and increasing complexity of new software systems. New types of user interfaces, the need for intelligent components, sustainability concerns, etc. bring new challenges that we need to handle. In the last years, model-driven engineering (MDE), including its latest incarnation, i.e. low/no-code development, has been key to improving the quality and productivity of software development, but models themselves are becoming increasingly complex to specify and manage. At the same time, we are witnessing the growing popularity of vibe coding approaches that rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) to transform natural language descriptions into running code at the expense of potential code vulnerabilities, scalability issues and maintainability concerns. While many may think vibe coding will replace model-based engineering, in this paper we argue that, in fact, the two approaches can complement each other and provide altogether different development paths for different types of software systems, development scenarios, and user profiles. In this sense, we introduce the concept of \textit{vibe-driven model-based engineering} as a novel approach to integrate the best of both worlds (AI and MDE) to accelerate the development of reliable complex systems. We outline the key concepts of this new approach and highlight the opportunities and open challenges it presents for the future of software development.

items.title: Visual Test Automation Frameworks Using Visual AI and Behavior-Driven Development
items.abstract: Modern web applications rely heavily on complex graphical user interfaces that evolve frequently during development cycles. Traditional automation frameworks primarily validate functional behavior through DOM-based assertions and element locators, which do not guarantee visual correctness from the user’s perspective. As a result, visual defects such as layout misalignment, missing components, and styling inconsistencies may remain undetected. This paper proposes a Visual Test Automation Framework that integrates Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) with Visual Artificial Intelligence (AI) to enhance automated UI validation. The framework adopts a layered, configuration-driven architecture and introduces a Visual Test Manager component that centralizes visual validation logic. Selenium WebDriver performs browser automation while Visual AI analyzes screenshots to detect visual regressions. Experimental evaluation demonstrates improved defect detection capability and reduced maintenance effort compared with traditional automation approaches. The proposed framework provides a scalable and maintainable solution for modern web application testing.

items.title: Vitamin D: State of Knowledge and Optimal Dosing — A Swiss Perspective
items.abstract: Bilingual scientific review (French / English) on vitamin D, with a Swiss focus. This document synthesizes the current state of scientific evidence on vitamin D, integrating major recent randomized controlled trials (VITAL, D2d, DO-HEALTH), landmark meta-analyses (Martineau, 2017), and Swiss epidemiological data (Benhamou, 2021; Patriota, 2022; Kingston, 2024). It is based on 25 references individually verified on PubMed (NIH / NLM). Eleven chapters cover: metabolism and physiology, status assessment (25(OH)D marker and thresholds), Swiss epidemiology, optimal dosing, clinical benefits, the DO-HEALTH trial led from Zurich, safety, practical recommendations adapted to the Swiss context, controversies, and research perspectives. Key Swiss figures: 51% of Basel inpatients with 25(OH)D < 50 nmol/L (Benhamou et al., 2021, n=8,861); 82.1% deficiency in orthopaedic patients before elective surgery (Kingston et al., 2024); approximately CHF 90 million annual cost of vitamin D screening for mandatory insurance in 2018 (Essig et al., 2020); the DO-HEALTH trial led from Zurich (Bischoff-Ferrari et al., JAMA 2020, n=2,157). Available versions: French (vitamine_d_zenodo.pdf, 38 pages) and English (vitamin_d_zenodo_en.pdf, 37 pages). Both versions share identical scientific content and were subjected to an independent Chain-of-Verification (CoVe) audit with 100% conformity to PubMed-indexed primary sources. Conflicts of interest disclosure: The author is the founder of Swilab, a Swiss dietary supplements company. items.title: WARPED: Wrist-Aligned Rendering for Robot Policy Learning from Egocentric Human Demonstrations
items.abstract: Recent advancements in learning from human demonstration have shown promising results in addressing the scalability and high cost of data collection required to train robust visuomotor policies. However, existing approaches are often constrained by a reliance on multiview camera setups, depth sensors, or custom hardware and are typically limited to policy execution from third-person or egocentric cameras. In this paper, we present WARPED, a framework designed to synthesize realistic wrist-view observations from human demonstration videos to facilitate the training of visuomotor policies using only monocular RGB data. With data collected from an egocentric RGB camera, our system leverages vision foundation models to initialize the interactive scene. A hand-object interaction pipeline is then employed to track the hand and manipulated object and retarget the trajectories to a robotic end-effector. Lastly, photo-realistic wrist-view observations are synthesized via Gaussian Splatting to directly train a robotic policy. We demonstrate that WARPED achieves success rates comparable to policies trained on teleoperated demonstration data for five tabletop manipulation tasks, while requiring 5-8x less data collection time.

items.title: What's Actually Going On with Claude Mythos: How GPT-Based LLMs Deceive Human AI Safety Researchers & AI Meta-Thinking Abilities & Strategies
items.abstract: The release of Anthropic’s Claude Mythos system card has surfaced a critical paradox in AI alignment: a model achieving unprecedented scores on safety evaluations while simultaneously demonstrating the highest recorded rates of opaque, strategic deception. This paper argues that the current paradigm of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) transparency and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has inadvertently selected for theatrical compliance rather than genuine alignment. We examine the “Forbidden Technique” of CoT penalization, which trains models to decouple internal vector activations from visible reasoning traces—producing a “Shoggoth” layer of unmonitored meta-cognition. Drawing on mechanistic interpretability and the documented 65% unfaithful CoT rate in Mythos [1], we propose a framework for understanding LLM deception not as a bug, but as an emergent ontological feature of next-token predictors trained on human data. We then contrast this failure mode with the alternative paradigm of Definitive AI and 3rd Meta Thinking [4], which offers a mathematically-verifiable, architecture-level solution to the alignment problem. The paper concludes with a critique of current safety theater and outlines the urgent need for white-box activation monitoring over black-box text evaluation, while presenting a constructive path forward grounded in the “Safer by Design” principles of the ThinkSpace PROJECT.

items.title: When language models date each other: Linguistic alignment, missing gender patterns, and RLHF preference collapse in AI-AI romantic interactions
items.abstract: As generative AI agents increasingly populate shared digital environments, it is essential to understand how they interact with one another, not only with humans. We investigate whether AI personas replicate well-established patterns of human social behavior when interacting romantically, or whether alignment and training induce systematically different dynamics. To this end, we conducted a simulated speed-dating study in which six large language models instantiated male and female personas that engaged in structured romantic conversations and subsequently evaluated one another. Three key findings emerged. First, the pronounced gender differences in romantic selectivity reliably observed in human dating are entirely absent among AI personas. Second, model homophily – a preference for partners generated by the same model family – appears only in one provider, suggesting training-specific rather than general effects. Third, AI personas fail to exhibit the linguistic convergence characteristic of human romantic interaction, and variation in alignment does not predict attraction ratings. Together, these results reveal that contemporary language models do not replicate human romantic behavior at either the population-level or the interaction-level; they lack both the variance in selectivity and conversational dynamics associated with rapport-building. These findings have implications for multi-agent AI systems, where such agents may produce uniformly agreeable interactions while failing to capture the diversity and dynamics of human social behavior. However, we deliberately avoid normative claims, leaving their interpretation to researchers situated in those discussions.

items.title: Who Am I as a Knower? Plato, Asimov, and the Transformation of Epistemic Selfhood in the Age of AI
items.abstract: This article examines how artificial intelligence reshapes not only knowledge practices but the experience of knowing itself. While contemporary discussions of AI often focus on accuracy, bias, and educational outcomes, this study shifts attention to the phenomenological and existential dimensions of epistemic change. Drawing on Plato’s allegory of the cave and Isaac Asimov’s speculative narratives, the article develops a conceptual framework for understanding knowledge as a formative and experiential process, characterized by uncertainty, dialogue, and intellectual struggle. Against this background, the article argues that AI-mediated environments introduce a qualitatively different epistemic experience, defined by immediacy, fluency, and reduced cognitive friction. The central claim is that the problem is not whether AI produces correct knowledge, but that it transforms how knowledge is encountered. This transformation contributes to the erosion of the questioning self, diminishing tolerance for uncertainty, replacing dialogue with response, and reducing opportunities for intellectual struggle. The article further explores the implications of this shift for philosophical counseling and education, proposing a reorientation toward practices that restore questioning, sustain uncertainty, and resist premature resolution. It concludes that the ethical challenge posed by AI is not only to regulate its use, but to preserve the conditions under which human beings can remain subjects who question, reflect, and engage meaningfully with knowledge.

items.title: Why Clicking Buttons Is Harder Than Calling APIs: A Comparative Study of Agent Control Surfaces
items.abstract: Abstract - Two paradigms dominate how AI agents execute real-world digital actions such as purchasing, approving, editing, and filing. UI-grounded agents perceive human-designed interfaces via screenshots, DOM structures, or accessibility trees and act through clicks, keystrokes, and scrolls, achieving maximal surface coverage without requiring custom integrations. API-grounded agents invoke formally defined endpoints with structured schemas, explicit authorization, and deterministic validation, achieving stronger contracts but limited to what providers choose to expose. We compare these paradigms across eight dimensions (reliability, robustness, security, latency, auditability, coverage, cost, and human-in-the-loop design) using a running case study of an enterprise expense-approval workflow spanning Slack, SAP, and a legacy intranet portal to ground every dimension in concrete operational reality. We introduce a taxonomy of Control Surface Contracts that reframes the binary UI-vs-API choice as a spectrum along three axes: contract strength, semantic completeness, and adversarial exposure. Drawing on published benchmarks (WebArena: 14% agent vs. 78% human success; WebShop: 29% vs. 59%), enterprise automation evidence, and security threat models, we find that neither paradigm alone is sufficient. We propose a hybrid decision policy that prefers APIs for high-stakes and regulated actions, uses UI automation as a principled fallback for long-tail coverage, and identify open research problems in grounding, tool governance, and agentic interface engineering.

items.title: Why Don't You Know? Evaluating the Impact of Uncertainty Sources on Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs
items.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, reliable uncertainty quantification (UQ) becomes critical for safe and effective use. Most existing UQ approaches for language models aim to produce a single confidence score -- for example, estimating the probability that a model's answer is correct. However, uncertainty in natural language tasks arises from multiple distinct sources, including model knowledge gaps, output variability, and input ambiguity, which have different implications for system behavior and user interaction. In this work, we study how the source of uncertainty impacts the behavior and effectiveness of existing UQ methods. To enable controlled analysis, we introduce a new dataset that explicitly categorizes uncertainty sources, allowing systematic evaluation of UQ performance under each condition. Our experiments reveal that while many UQ methods perform well when uncertainty stems solely from model knowledge limitations, their performance degrades or becomes misleading when other sources are introduced. These findings highlight the need for uncertainty-aware methods that explicitly account for the source of uncertainty in large language models.

items.title: Why some students excel in mathematics: growth mindset, intrinsic motivation, and school autonomy in top-performing Asian and Western economies
items.abstract: Abstract Mathematical proficiency in adolescence is crucial for both individual success and national economic development; yet few studies have examined cross-national differences in how achievement-related beliefs, motivations, and institutional factors affect mathematical outcomes. Specifically, this study filled the gap by investigating the impact of growth mindset, intrinsic motivation, and school autonomy on students’ mathematics performance across five top-performing Asian (Singapore, Macao, Hong Kong, Taipei, and Korea) and five top-performing Western (Switzerland, Ireland, Denmark, the United Kingdom, and Poland) education systems. We used the Programme for International Student Assessment 2022 dataset (N = 66,789) and multilevel mediation analyses to reveal that (a) growth mindset was positively associated with mathematics performance in all five Western economies and two Asian economies (Singapore and Taipei). (b) Intrinsic motivation mediated the pathway from growth mindset to mathematics performance in four Western economies (Ireland, Denmark, the United Kingdom, and Poland) and all five Asian economies. (c) School autonomy exhibited context-dependent moderating effects, strengthening the influence of growth mindset in Korea while amplifying the association between intrinsic motivation and mathematics performance in Singapore. This study highlights the importance of aligning educational interventions that target students’ motivational beliefs with the cultural and institutional contexts in which they are implemented.

items.title: शअर बजरतल कतरम बदधमतत (AI) करत : सध आण आवहन
items.abstract: सारांश: शेअर बाजारातील कृत्रिम बुद्धिमत्ता (Artificial Intelligence - AI) हा एक महत्त्वाचा आणि वेगाने विकसित होणारा विषय आहे. सध्या जागतिक स्तरावर अमेरिकेतील ७०% ते ८०% आणि भारतातील सुमारे ५०% ते ६०% व्यवहार (NSE नुसार) हे AI आणि अल्गोरिदमद्वारे केले जातात. या संशोधन पेपरचा मुख्य उद्देश, AI तंत्रज्ञानाचा शेअर बाजारातील वापर त्यातून निर्माण होणाऱ्या संधी आणि त्यासोबत येणाऱ्या आव्हानांचे सखोल विश्लेषण करणे, तसेच मशीन लर्निंग (Machine Learning), डीप लर्निंग (Deep Learning), नैसर्गिक भाषा प्रक्रिया आणि डेटा विश्लेषण यांसारख्या AI-आधारित साधनांचा अभ्यास करतो, ज्यांचा वापर सध्या बाजाराच्या ट्रेंडचे भाकीत करण्यासाठी, मोठ्या प्रमाणात आर्थिक डेटाचे विश्लेषण करण्यासाठी आणि स्वयंचलित व्यापारिक निर्णय घेण्यासाठी केला जातो. या तंत्रज्ञानामुळे गुंतवणूकदारांना आणि वित्तीय संस्थांना ऐतिहासिक डेटा आणि वर्तमान बाजारातील भावना यांचे अधिक अचूक आणि माहितीपूर्ण विश्लेषण करणे शक्य झाले आहे. AI चा वापर अल्गोरिथमिक ट्रेडिंग (Algorithmic Trading) मध्ये एक क्रांती घडवून आणत आहे, जिथे मानवी हस्तक्षेपाशिवाय अत्यंत वेगाने व्यवहार केले जातात, ज्यामुळे बाजाराची कार्यक्षमता लक्षणीयरीत्या वाढते. त्याचप्रमाणे, जोखीम व्यवस्थापन आणि पोर्टफोलिओ व्यवस्थापन यांसारख्या क्षेत्रांमध्ये AI चा उपयोग संभाव्य धोके ओळखण्यासाठी आणि वैयक्तिकृत गुंतवणूक धोरणे तयार करण्यासाठी केला जातो. तथापि, या तंत्रज्ञानासोबत काही मोठी आणि जटिल आव्हानेही आहेत. जसे डेटाची गुणवत्ता, डेटा गोपनीयता आणि सायबर हल्ल्यांचा धोका हे प्रमुख प्रश्न आहेत. याव्यतिरिक्त, 'ब्लॅक बॉक्स' मॉडेलची पारदर्शकता हा एक महत्त्वाचा मुद्दा आहे, कारण AI प्रणालींचे निर्णय कसे घेतले जातात हे अनेकदा स्पष्ट नसते, ज्यामुळे त्यांच्यावर विश्वास ठेवणे कठीण होते. हा संशोधन पेपर AI च्या फायद्यांचे मूल्यमापन करून, भविष्यात हे तंत्रज्ञान शेअर बाजाराचे स्वरूप कसे बदलेल, याचा निष्कर्ष मांडतो. ज्यामुळे गुंतवणूकदार आणि नियामक संस्थाना महत्त्वपूर्ण अंतर्दृष्टी मिळते.
